title: Rotational Dynamics

toc.title: 3.1 Moment of inertia of a uniform rod and radius of gyration
3.2 Torque, rotational work, kinetic energy and power

html:
Rotational dynamics is linear dynamics re-written for turning: force becomes torque, mass becomes moment of inertia, momentum becomes angular momentum. Of the 10 Mechanics questions, with about 1 questions from this chapter.

The MEC syllabus limits moment of inertia to the uniform rigid rod, so expect a rod about its centre or its end, a radius of gyration, a torque or rotational-power calculation, or a conservation-of-angular-momentum situation such as a spinning skater.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • Rod: I = ML^2/12 about a perpendicular axis through the centre, ML^2/3 through an end; the ratio is 4.
  • Radius of gyration k = \sqrt{I/M}: L/(2\sqrt{3}) about the centre, L/\sqrt{3} about an end.
  • Parallel-axis theorem I = I_{cm} + Md^2; what I depends on (and that it does not depend on \omega).
  • Torque \tau = rF\sin\theta and \tau = I\alpha; rotational work \tau\theta, power \tau\omega, kinetic energy \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2.
  • Angular momentum L = I\omega, \tau = dL/dt; with no external torque I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2.
  • K = L^2/2I: when a skater pulls in, \omega and K rise while L stays the same.

3.1 Moment of inertia of a uniform rod and radius of gyration

Moment of inertia

Moment of inertia

The moment of inertia of a body about an axis is the sum of the products of the mass of each particle and the square of its perpendicular distance from the axis: I = \sum m_ir_i^2 (or \int r^2\,dm).

It measures the body's opposition to a change in its rotational motion about that axis. SI unit kg m²; dimensions [ML^2].

I plays in rotation the part that mass plays in translation. Unlike mass, it is not fixed for a body: it depends on

  1. the mass of the body,
  2. how that mass is distributed about the axis (mass far from the axis counts much more, because of r^2),
  3. the position and orientation of the axis.

It does not depend on the angular velocity or on the torque applied (for a rigid body).

The uniform rod

Take a thin uniform rod of mass M and length L, so its mass per unit length is M/L. A slice of length dx at distance x from the axis has mass dm = (M/L)\,dx and contributes x^2\,dm.

  • Axis through the centre, perpendicular to the rod: x runs from -L/2 to +L/2, and I = \frac{M}{L}\int x^2\,dx = \frac{M}{L}\cdot\frac{L^3}{12}.
  • Axis through one end, perpendicular to the rod: x runs from 0 to L, and I = \frac{M}{L}\cdot\frac{L^3}{3}.

I_{centre} = \frac{ML^2}{12}, \qquad I_{end} = \frac{ML^2}{3} = 4\,I_{centre}

Axis of the rod (mass M, length L) Moment of inertia Radius of gyration k
Perpendicular, through the centre ML^2/12 (the least for a perpendicular axis) L/(2\sqrt{3}) \approx 0.289L
Perpendicular, through one end ML^2/3 L/\sqrt{3} \approx 0.577L
Perpendicular, at distance d from the centre ML^2/12 + Md^2 \sqrt{L^2/12 + d^2}
Through the centre, at angle \theta to the rod (ML^2/12)\sin^2\theta (L\sin\theta)/(2\sqrt{3})
Along the rod itself (thin rod) \approx 0 \approx 0

Two theorems

  • Parallel-axis theorem: I = I_{cm} + Md^2, where I_{cm} is about a parallel axis through the centre of mass and d is the distance between the axes. The centre-of-mass axis therefore gives the least moment of inertia of all parallel axes. Check: \frac{ML^2}{12} + M\left(\frac{L}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{ML^2}{3}.
  • Perpendicular-axis theorem (plane lamina only): I_z = I_x + I_y, where x and y lie in the plane of the lamina and z is perpendicular to it, all three meeting at one point.

Radius of gyration

Radius of gyration

The radius of gyration k of a body about an axis is the distance from the axis at which, if the whole mass of the body were concentrated, it would have the same moment of inertia: I = Mk^2, so k = \sqrt{I/M}.

It is the root-mean-square distance of the body's particles from the axis. SI unit: metre.

k depends on the axis and on the distribution of mass, but not on the total mass (doubling the mass of a rod doubles I and leaves k the same).

For reference, when a question gives a wheel instead of a rod: ring about its axis MR^2 (k = R), disc MR^2/2, solid sphere about a diameter \frac{2}{5}MR^2, thin spherical shell \frac{2}{3}MR^2.

For the same mass and radius a ring has a larger I than a disc, because all its mass is at the rim — the reason a flywheel has a heavy rim.

Worked example 3.1 — a rod and a dumb-bell

Problem.(a) A uniform rod of mass 1 kg and length 1.2 m. Find I about perpendicular axes through its centre and through one end, and k about the end.(b) Two 2 kg balls are fixed at the ends of a light rod 1 m long. Find I about a perpendicular axis through the centre.

Solution.(a) I_c = 1(1.2)^2/12 = 0.12\ \text{kg m}^2; I_e = 4I_c = 0.48\ \text{kg m}^2; k_e = L/\sqrt{3} = 1.2/1.732 = 0.69\ \text{m}.(b) Each ball is 0.5 m from the axis: I = 2\times2(0.5)^2 = 1.0\ \text{kg m}^2. A uniform rod of the same total mass (4 kg) would have only 4(1)^2/12 = 0.33\ \text{kg m}^2 — mass at the ends counts more.

Square roots and squares

I_{end} = 4I_{centre}, but k_{end} = 2k_{centre} (because k \propto \sqrt{I}). And the parallel-axis theorem adds Md^2 only from the centre-of-mass axis: you cannot go from the end axis to another axis by adding Md^2 — go back to the centre first.

3.2 Torque, rotational work, kinetic energy and power

Torque

Torque

The torque (moment of a force) about an axis is the turning effect of the force: \vec\tau = \vec r\times\vec F, of magnitude \tau = rF\sin\theta = F\,r_\perp, where r_\perp = r\sin\theta is the perpendicular distance of the line of action of the force from the axis (the moment arm). SI unit N m; dimensions [ML^2T^{-2}].

  • The direction of \vec\tau is along the axis, given by the right-hand rule (anticlockwise torque is taken positive by convention).
  • A force through the axis, or along \vec r, gives zero torque. A door handle is far from the hinges so that a small force gives a large torque.
  • A couple (two equal, opposite, parallel forces F a distance d apart) has zero net force and torque Fd about every point: it turns without translating.
  • Torque and work share the unit N m and the dimensions [ML^2T^{-2}], but torque is a vector and is never written in joules.

Newton's second law for rotation

For a rigid body turning about a fixed axis, \tau = I\alpha — the rotational form of F = ma. For constant \alpha the rotational equations of motion are exact copies of the linear ones:

Linear Rotational Link
displacement s angle \theta (rad) s = r\theta
velocity v angular velocity \omega v = r\omega
acceleration a angular acceleration \alpha a_t = r\alpha
mass m moment of inertia I I = \sum mr^2
force F = ma torque \tau = I\alpha \tau = rF\sin\theta
momentum p = mv angular momentum L = I\omega L = rp\sin\theta
v = u + at \omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t
s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2 \theta = \omega_0t + \frac{1}{2}\alpha t^2
v^2 = u^2 + 2as \omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha\theta
work W = Fs work W = \tau\theta
kinetic energy \frac{1}{2}mv^2 kinetic energy \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2
power P = Fv power P = \tau\omega

Number of revolutions n = \theta/2\pi; \omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi N/60 for N rpm.

Rotational work, kinetic energy and power

  • Work done by a constant torque turning a body through angle \theta: W = \tau\theta (in radians).
  • Rotational kinetic energy: K = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2 — the sum of \frac{1}{2}mv^2 over all particles, with v = r\omega.
  • Work–energy theorem for rotation: net work by torques = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2 - \frac{1}{2}I\omega_0^2.
  • Power: P = \tau\omega. A motor that gives torque 20 N m at 300 rpm delivers 20\times2\pi\times5 = 628\ \text{W}.
  • Rolling without slipping (wheel, ball): v = R\omega and K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 + \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\left(1 + \frac{k^2}{R^2}\right). Part of the energy is always rotational, so a rolling body accelerates down a slope more slowly than one sliding without friction.
Worked example 3.2 — torque, work and energy

Problem. A constant torque of 10 N m acts for 5 s on a wheel with I = 2\ \text{kg m}^2, starting from rest. Find the angular acceleration, the final angular velocity, the angle turned and the kinetic energy gained.

Solution. \alpha = \tau/I = 5\ \text{rad s}^{-2}; \omega = \alpha t = 25\ \text{rad s}^{-1}; \theta = \frac{1}{2}\alpha t^2 = 62.5\ \text{rad}; K = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = \frac{1}{2}(2)(625) = 625\ \text{J}.

Check by work \tau\theta = 10\times62.5 = 625\ \text{J}.

Worked example 3.3 — a rod swinging down

Problem. A uniform rod of length 1.2 m is pivoted freely at one end and released from rest in the horizontal position (g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}). Find(a) its angular acceleration just after release and(b) its angular velocity as it passes the vertical.

Solution.(a) The weight acts at the centre, L/2 from the pivot: \alpha = \frac{Mg(L/2)}{ML^2/3} = \frac{3g}{2L} = 12.5\ \text{rad s}^{-2}. (The free end then starts with acceleration \alpha L = \frac{3}{2}g — more than g.)(b) The centre falls L/2: Mg\frac{L}{2} = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{ML^2}{3}\omega^2, so \omega = \sqrt{3g/L} = \sqrt{25} = 5\ \text{rad s}^{-1}; the tip moves at \omega L = 6\ \text{m s}^{-1}.

Rods in a hurry

Rod about its end: I = ML^2/3, weight acting at L/2. Released from horizontal: \alpha = 3g/2L, \omega_{bottom} = \sqrt{3g/L}, tip speed \sqrt{3gL}. The mass cancels in all three — if an option contains M, it is wrong.

3.3 Angular momentum and its conservation

Angular momentum

The angular momentum of a particle about a point is the moment of its linear momentum: \vec L = \vec r\times\vec p, of magnitude L = mvr\sin\theta = mv\,r_\perp. For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, L = I\omega.

SI unit kg m² s⁻¹ = J s; dimensions [ML^2T^{-1}], the same as Planck's constant.

Even a particle moving in a straight line has angular momentum about a point not on that line: L = mvd, where d is the perpendicular distance of the line from the point. If no force acts, v and d stay fixed, so L is constant.

Torque and angular momentum. Newton's second law for rotation in its general form is

\vec\tau = \frac{d\vec L}{dt}

A torque acting for a time \Delta t gives an angular impulse \tau\,\Delta t = \Delta L.

Principle of conservation of angular momentum

If the net external torque on a system is zero, its total angular momentum is constant: I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2. A body that changes its own shape (and so its I) changes its angular velocity in inverse proportion.

Situation What happens and why
Ice skater or ballet dancer pulls the arms in I falls, so \omega rises; arms out again slows the spin
Diver or gymnast tucks the body I falls, more somersaults in the air; opens out to slow before entering the water
Person on a rotating stool pulls dumb-bells inward the stool spins faster
Planet nearer the Sun moves faster gravity is a central force (zero torque about the Sun); mvr constant — this is Kepler's second law (equal areas in equal times)
A star collapses into a neutron star its radius shrinks enormously, so it spins very fast
If the Earth shrank with no change of mass I \propto R^2, so the day would shorten as R^2
Helicopter tail rotor its sideways thrust supplies the torque that stops the body spinning opposite to the main rotor

Energy is not conserved in the same way. Since K = \frac{L^2}{2I}, with L fixed the kinetic energy is inversely proportional to I. When the skater pulls in, K increases — the extra energy is the work her muscles do pulling the arms in.

When a non-rotating disc is dropped onto a spinning one and they turn together, L is conserved but kinetic energy is lost (to friction between the discs), just as in a perfectly inelastic collision.

Worked example 3.4 — a skater and the Earth

Problem.(a) A skater spinning at 2 rad s⁻¹ with I = 4\ \text{kg m}^2 pulls her arms in to make I = 1.6\ \text{kg m}^2. Find the new angular velocity and the ratio of final to initial kinetic energy.(b) If the Earth contracted to half its radius with no change of mass, how long would a day be?

Solution.(a) \omega_2 = I_1\omega_1/I_2 = 4(2)/1.6 = 5\ \text{rad s}^{-1}. K_2/K_1 = I_1/I_2 = 2.5 (from 8 J to 20 J).(b) I \propto R^2 falls to \frac{1}{4}, so \omega becomes 4 times and the period T = 24/4 = 6 hours.

Worked example 3.5 — two discs coupled

Problem. A disc with I_1 = 2\ \text{kg m}^2 spins at 10 rad s⁻¹. A second disc, I_2 = 3\ \text{kg m}^2, at rest, is dropped onto it on the same axle and they turn together. Find the common angular velocity and the kinetic energy lost.

Solution. \omega = I_1\omega_1/(I_1 + I_2) = 20/5 = 4\ \text{rad s}^{-1}. K_1 = \frac{1}{2}(2)(100) = 100\ \text{J}; K_2 = \frac{1}{2}(5)(16) = 40\ \text{J}: 60 J is lost — the fraction I_2/(I_1 + I_2) = 0.6.

Conserved does not mean unchanged

In a spin with no external torque, L is constant but \omega and K both change whenever I changes. Options that say "angular velocity unchanged" or "kinetic energy unchanged" for a skater pulling in her arms are the classic distractors.

Trap — same mass and radius does not mean same moment of inertia

About an axis through the centre: ring MR² > disc ½MR² > solid sphere (2/5)MR².

What matters is how far the mass sits from the axis, not merely how much mass there is — hence in a race down an incline the solid sphere wins and the ring comes last, all with the same M and R. Also keep separate: radius of gyration (k, defined by I = Mk²) is not a physical radius of the body.

Formula and fact sheet

Quantity Formula SI unit and dimensions

Rod, centre (perpendicular) ML^2/12; k = L/(2\sqrt{3}) = 0.289L
Rod, end (perpendicular) ML^2/3; k = L/\sqrt{3} = 0.577L
Rod, distance d from centre ML^2/12 + Md^2
Rod through centre at angle \theta (ML^2/12)\sin^2\theta

Torque \tau = rF\sin\theta = Fr_\perp = I\alpha; couple Fd N m, [ML^2T^{-2}]

Rotational work and power W = \tau\theta; P = \tau\omega J; W
Rotational KE K = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = L^2/2I J

Chapter summary

  • Moment of inertia I = \sum mr^2 depends on the mass, its distribution and the axis — not on the angular velocity; it is the rotational analogue of mass.
  • Uniform rod: ML^2/12 about the centre, ML^2/3 about an end; the centre gives the least I of all parallel axes (I = I_{cm} + Md^2).
  • Radius of gyration k = \sqrt{I/M}: L/(2\sqrt{3}) about the centre and L/\sqrt{3} about an end; k doubles when I quadruples.
  • Torque \tau = rF\sin\theta (unit N m, never joule) and \tau = I\alpha; a force through the axis gives no torque; a couple turns without translating.
  • Rotational work \tau\theta, power \tau\omega, kinetic energy \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2; rotational equations of motion mirror the linear ones.
  • Angular momentum L = I\omega = mvr\sin\theta (J s); \tau = dL/dt.
  • With zero external torque I\omega is constant: the skater, the diver, planets moving faster near the Sun; K = L^2/2I rises when I falls.

Answers and explanations — Set A

1. (b) — I = \sum mr^2: kilogram × metre². N m is the unit of torque.

2. (a) — I = \frac{M}{L}\int_{-L/2}^{L/2}x^2\,dx = ML^2/12.

3. (c) — ML^2/12 + M(L/2)^2 = ML^2/3, four times the value about the centre.

4. (d) — k = \sqrt{I/M} = \sqrt{L^2/12} = L/(2\sqrt{3}) \approx 0.29L. L/\sqrt{3} is the value about an end.

5. (a) — I depends on the mass, its distribution and the axis; for a rigid body it is the same at any angular velocity.

6. (b) — I = I_{cm} + Md^2; the term is always added, so the centre-of-mass axis gives the least value.

7. (c) — I resists angular acceleration (\tau = I\alpha) as mass resists linear acceleration (F = ma).

8. (a) — \tau = I\alpha is the rotational form of F = ma; angular momentum is the analogue of momentum.

9. (d) — \tau = rF: [L][MLT^{-2}] = [ML^2T^{-2}], the same as work, though torque is a vector.

10. (c) — L = I\omega: kg m² s⁻¹ = (kg m² s⁻²) s = J s. J s⁻¹ is the watt.

11. (a) — summing \frac{1}{2}mv^2 with v = r\omega gives \frac{1}{2}(\sum mr^2)\omega^2 = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2.

12. (c) — P = dW/dt = \tau\,d\theta/dt = \tau\omega, the analogue of P = Fv.

13. (b) — W = \tau\theta with \theta in radians, the analogue of W = Fs.

14. (a) — \tau_{ext} = dL/dt, so zero external torque keeps L constant. Zero net force conserves linear momentum.

15. (c) — \tau = dL/dt is the general form of Newton's second law for rotation.

16. (d) — I\omega stays constant (no external torque about the vertical axis); pulling the arms in lowers I, so \omega rises.

17. (c) — a cross product is perpendicular to the plane containing \vec r and \vec F (right-hand rule); it lies along the axis of rotation.

18. (b) — the two forces of a couple add to zero (no translation) but their torque Fd is not zero.

19. (a) — K = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = \frac{(I\omega)^2}{2I} = \frac{L^2}{2I}, like K = p^2/2m.

20. (d) — k = \sqrt{I/M}; the mass cancels, so k depends only on how the mass is spread about the chosen axis.

21. (b) — angular momentum I\omega corresponds to linear momentum mv.

Answers and explanations — Set B

1. (b) — \frac{ML^2/3}{ML^2/12} = 4.

2. (c) — k \propto \sqrt{I}, so the ratio is \sqrt{4} = 2 (L/\sqrt{3} against L/2\sqrt{3}). The tempting 4 is the ratio of the moments of inertia.

3. (d) — by the parallel-axis theorem I = ML^2/12 + Md^2 grows with d; the end (d = L/2) is farthest. About its own length a thin rod has almost no I.

4. (a) — K = L^2/2I; with I fixed, doubling L makes K four times.

5. (b) — no external torque, so L is constant; I falls, so \omega rises and K = L^2/2I increases (her muscles do the work).

6. (c) — \tau = Fr_\perp; a larger moment arm gives more torque from the same push.

7. (b) — the moment arm r_\perp is zero, so \tau = Fr_\perp = 0 (e.g. pulling a door straight toward the hinge).

8. (a) — tucking brings mass close to the axis, lowering I; with L constant, \omega increases. L itself cannot change in mid-air (no external torque about the centre of mass).

9. (c) — zero net force means no acceleration of the centre of mass; a non-zero torque gives \alpha = \tau/I. A couple is the example.

10. (d) — the Sun's pull is central, so it exerts no torque about the Sun; L = mvr_\perp stays constant, which is the equal-areas law (areal speed = L/2m), and v rises as r falls. Kinetic energy is not constant — it changes as the planet speeds up.

11. (a) — k = L/(2\sqrt{3}) for both: the radius of gyration does not depend on the mass.

12. (c) — I \propto R^2 falls to one quarter, so \omega rises four times and the period falls from 24 h to 6 h. (b) uses I \propto R.

13. (d) — K = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2 with the same \omega, so K \propto I: \frac{ML^2/3}{ML^2/12} = 4.

Answers and explanations — Set C

1. (c) — I = ML^2/3 = 1(1.44)/3 = 0.48 kg m². 0.12 kg m² is the value about the centre.

2. (a) — each ball is 0.5 m from the axis: I = 2\times2\times0.5^2 = 1.0 kg m². (d) uses 1 m instead of 0.5 m.

3. (d) — \alpha = \tau/I = 5 rad s⁻²; \omega = \alpha t = 25 rad s⁻¹; K = \frac{1}{2}(2)(25)^2 = 625 J (equals \tau\theta = 10\times62.5).

4. (b) — Mg\frac{L}{2} = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{ML^2}{3}\omega^2 gives \omega = \sqrt{3g/L} = \sqrt{30/1.2} = 5 rad s⁻¹. 6 is the tip speed in m s⁻¹.

5. (c) — \omega = 2\pi(300/60) = 10\pi rad s⁻¹; P = \tau\omega = 20\times31.4 = 628 W. (b) multiplies by rpm without converting.

6. (d) — \omega_2 = I_1\omega_1/I_2 = 8/1.6 = 5 rad s⁻¹. (a) inverts the ratio.

7.(a) — \tau = rF\sin\theta = 0.4\times50\times\sin30^{\circ} = 10 N m.(b) uses \cos30^{\circ};(c) assumes the force is perpendicular.

8. (b) — k = L/\sqrt{3} = 60/1.732 = 34.6 cm. 17.3 cm is the value about the centre.

9. (d) — \omega = 20/5 = 4 rad s⁻¹; KE falls from \frac{1}{2}(2)(100) = 100 J to \frac{1}{2}(5)(16) = 40 J, a loss of 60 J. (b) is the final KE, not the loss.

10. (c) — \alpha = \frac{Mg(L/2)}{ML^2/3} = \frac{3g}{2L}, so the end has a = \alpha L = \frac{3}{2}g = 15 m s⁻² — more than g, which is why (b) is the trap.

Group D — Model answers for long questions (10 marks each, for deeper revision)

  1. Define torque, moment of inertia and angular momentum. State the law of conservation of angular momentum with examples and solve a numerical. [10]
  2. State the parallel and perpendicular axis theorems and find the moment of inertia of a disc. Explain rolling motion with a numerical. [10]

Model answer D1: torque, moment of inertia and conservation of angular momentum (10 marks)

Introduction. Rotational motion has quantities that match linear motion. Torque \vec\tau = \vec r\times\vec F turns a body, the moment of inertia I = \sum mr^2 resists the turning, and angular momentum \vec L = I\vec\omega measures the quantity of rotation.

Relations.

  1. Torque. \tau = rF\sin\theta, in newton metre. It is zero if the force passes through the axis.
  2. Newton's law for rotation. \tau = I\alpha, the counterpart of F = ma.
  3. Angular momentum. For a particle \vec L = \vec r\times\vec p, and for a rigid body L = I\omega.
  4. Torque as rate of change. \vec\tau = d\vec L/dt. If \vec\tau = 0 then \vec L is constant. This is the law of conservation of angular momentum.
  5. Rotational kinetic energy. K = \tfrac12I\omega^2 = L^2/2I.

Examples of the law.

  • A skater or diver pulls in the arms or legs, so I falls and \omega rises.
  • A person on a rotating turntable holding weights changes the speed by moving the weights.
  • Planets move faster near the sun (perihelion), which is Kepler's second law.
  • A helicopter needs a tail rotor so that the reaction torque does not spin the body.
Linear Rotational
v = u + at \omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t
s = ut + \tfrac12at^2 \theta = \omega_0t + \tfrac12\alpha t^2
F = ma \tau = I\alpha
p = mv L = I\omega

Numerical. A skater spins at 2\ \text{rev s}^{-1} with I = 3.0\ \text{kg m}^2. She pulls her arms in and I becomes 1.0\ \text{kg m}^2. Then I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2 gives \omega_2 = 3\times2 = 6\ \text{rev s}^{-1}.

The kinetic energy rises from \tfrac12(3)(4\pi)^2 = 237\ \text{J} to \tfrac12(1)(12\pi)^2 = 711\ \text{J}, three times larger, because her muscles do work.

Conclusion. With no external torque L stays constant, so a smaller moment of inertia means a faster spin.

Model answer D2: theorems of moment of inertia and rolling (10 marks)

Introduction. The moment of inertia depends on the axis. Two theorems let us find it for new axes from known values.

Theorems.

  1. Parallel axis theorem. I = I_{cm} + Md^2, where d is the distance between the axis and the parallel axis through the centre of mass. I_{cm} is always the smallest value.
  2. Perpendicular axis theorem (plane bodies only). I_z = I_x + I_y, where x and y are perpendicular axes in the plane and z is perpendicular to the plane.

Disc. For a uniform disc of mass M and radius R, about its central axis, I = \tfrac12MR^2. Using the perpendicular axis theorem with I_x = I_y, a diameter gives I_d = \tfrac14MR^2.

By the parallel axis theorem, the axis through the edge, perpendicular to the plane, has I = \tfrac12MR^2 + MR^2 = \tfrac32MR^2.

Body (axis) I
Ring (centre, perpendicular) MR^2
Disc (centre, perpendicular) \tfrac12MR^2
Solid sphere (diameter) \tfrac25MR^2
Hollow sphere (diameter) \tfrac23MR^2
Rod (centre) / (end) \dfrac{ML^2}{12} / \dfrac{ML^2}{3}

Rolling without slipping. The point of contact is at rest, so v = R\omega. The total kinetic energy is K = \tfrac12mv^2 + \tfrac12I\omega^2 = \tfrac12mv^2\left(1 + \dfrac{k^2}{R^2}\right), where k is the radius of gyration.

On an incline of height h, energy conservation gives v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2gh}{1 + k^2/R^2}}.

The acceleration is a = \dfrac{g\sin\theta}{1 + k^2/R^2}, so the order of arrival is solid sphere, disc, hollow sphere and ring, whatever their masses and radii.

Numerical. A disc (M = 2\ \text{kg}, R = 0.5\ \text{m}) has I = \tfrac12(2)(0.25) = 0.25\ \text{kg m}^2 about its axis.

A torque of 3\ \text{N m} gives \alpha = 12\ \text{rad s}^{-2}, and after 5\ \text{s}, \omega = 60\ \text{rad s}^{-1} and K = \tfrac12(0.25)(3600) = 450\ \text{J}.

Rolling down h = 3\ \text{m} (g = 10) it reaches v = \sqrt{2(10)(3)/1.5} = 6.3\ \text{m s}^{-1}, while a ring gets only \sqrt{30} = 5.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}.

Conclusion. Axis theorems extend known values of I, and a body with its mass closer to the axis rolls down faster.
